query: In conventional alloys, loss of toughness has long been associated with grain-boundary segregation and brittle grain-boundary precipitation. By contrast, compositionally complex high-entropy alloys can suppress rapid grain coarsening and deleterious intermetallic formation and have shown favorable strength–ductility combinations and resistance to high-temperature softening and low-temperature embrittlement. These findings do not establish what governs possible toughness degradation in an initially single-phase high-entropy alloy. Under the constraint of retaining a compositionally complex alloy suitable for demanding engineering service, what testable mechanistic hypothesis explains whether and why brittle behavior emerges? Specify a controlled comparison that would distinguish the hypothesis from conventional-alloy expectations, predicted observations relative to the initial baseline, its service and loading boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a decisive falsification outcome.

generation.hypothesis: In a single-phase high-entropy alloy, the emergence of brittle behavior is governed not by the formation of a second deleterious phase as in conventional alloys, but by the development of subtle, grain-boundary–localized compositional fluctuations (or short-range ordering) during service-relevant annealing that weaken grain-boundary cohesion.
generation.material_initial_state: A compositionally complex, single-phase HEA (e.g., an as-cast and rapidly quenched alloy) with a homogeneous distribution of all elements and no detectable grain-boundary precipitates.
generation.intervention: Perform a controlled thermal treatment that promotes modest atomic diffusion (e.g., an annealing step at a moderately elevated temperature for a prolonged time) on one set of specimens while retaining the rapid-solidification state in another set.
generation.conditions: Mechanical testing under quasi-static loading (e.g., uniaxial tensile or compressive tests) and scratch or indentation-based fracture toughness measurements conducted in the temperature range relevant to service (e.g., room temperature to 500 °C). Microstructural characterization via high-resolution TEM/atom-probe tomography and high-resolution EBSD will be used to detect local compositional fluctuations specifically at grain boundaries.
generation.structural_mediator: The appearance of nanoscale compositional clustering or short-range chemical ordering at grain boundaries without the formation of large second phases.
generation.mechanism: Subtle local diffusion during annealing drives the segregation of specific elements or induces short-range ordering near grain boundaries. This localized alteration in the chemical environment reduces cohesive bonding at the grain boundaries, leading to a drop in ductility and toughness even as the bulk remains a single phase. This mechanism contrasts with conventional alloys where grain-boundary embrittlement is typically driven by clearly separated brittle precipitates.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the baseline HEA (rapidly cooled homogeneous state), the annealed specimens are predicted to show reduced fracture toughness, a lower measured plastic strain before crack initiation, and an increased tendency for brittle intergranular fracture under service-relevant loading; microstructural analysis should reveal the presence of nanoscale compositional fluctuations or local ordering at grain boundaries in the annealed state.
generation.baseline: The as-cast, rapidly quenched single-phase HEA that exhibits a homogeneous microstructure and high toughness/ductility with no nanoscale compositional segregation or grain-boundary ordering.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis applies to HEAs maintained as single-phase alloys under service and loading conditions typical for demanding engineering applications (temperature range up to 500 °C and quasi-static loading). The hypothesis does not address behavior under extreme loading rates, irradiation environments, or when large-scale precipitates are deliberately introduced.
generation.uncertainty: The magnitude of toughness degradation due solely to subtle grain-boundary chemical heterogeneity is uncertain, and the specific kinetics of local ordering as a function of temperature/time may vary with alloy composition.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of HEA specimens: one set is rapidly cooled to preserve homogeneity, and the other is subjected to a controlled annealing treatment to promote atomic diffusion near grain boundaries. Characterize both sets with high-resolution TEM and atom-probe tomography to detect nanoscale compositional fluctuations at grain boundaries, and then perform fracture toughness and ductility tests under identical quasi-static loading and temperature conditions.
measurements: High-resolution TEM/atom-probe tomography for detecting grain-boundary compositional fluctuations or short-range ordering.
Quasi-static tensile/compressive tests to measure plastic strain and fracture toughness testing (via indentation or scratch methods) to quantify toughness differences.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the annealed specimens do not show evidence of nanoscale compositional fluctuations at grain boundaries AND do not exhibit a statistically significant decrease in toughness (or increase in brittle fracture behavior) relative to the rapidly quenched HEA, then the hypothesis is falsified.
